episode_title: Mark Stringer: Software Costs More Than We Want to Admit

real_qa.q: What characteristics define well-maintained software according to software delivery experts?
real_qa.r: Well-maintained software has a close connection with what users actually want to do and can do. It reflects a good model of the world and the way that the world works. The bits that get user attention are the ones that get the edges smoothed off them and become more effective, and it is comprehensible to the people maintaining it.

real_qa.q: Why does software become unmaintainable in organizations?
real_qa.r: Software becomes unmaintainable often due to organizational reasons involving a disconnect between understanding what is actually required from how the software will perform and arbitrary organizational requirements. The most common cause is trying to get things done by Christmas, where code is written in a hurry to meet deadlines, creating an organizational mismatch between what can actually be done in a particular time and what would be maintainable.

real_qa.q: What is the hidden cost that software developers and organizations avoid discussing?
real_qa.r: The real cost of software is how expensive it actually is. Developers and organizations dance around and do not want to mention the amazingly expensive nature of software. You do not get a lot of software for a million pounds, and people do not have any idea that some things are way more expensive than others, which results in people not making wise decisions about the software they actually want.

real_qa.q: How should software handovers be managed to ensure maintainability and future engagement?
real_qa.r: Comprehensive handovers should include written readme files for all software and for the roles being transitioned. The consultant spent six to eight weeks of handover with the incoming project manager, with similar efforts from design and tech lead perspectives. This painless handover to internal UK government department staff resulted in future work requests when they needed substantial pieces of work in that same area.

real_qa.q: What is the connection between cooperation and long-term success in software consulting relationships?
real_qa.r: Game theory tournaments show that cooperations will win out over strategies that are not cooperative. Finding anybody who will cooperate is a positive thing, even in competitive government environments with multiple suppliers. Being helpful during transitions and providing value creates positive outcomes both for the organization and the consulting firm, as demonstrated by return engagements and recommendations.

guest.bio_context: Mark Stringer has spent more than three decades working in the software industry, including delivering software for the UK government. He is the author of Delivering the Impossible, a book that explores how teams can better understand what's really happening inside their software project. He works with a small consultancy and has extensive experience in government software projects including the Animals and Science Licensing system.
